title: When do you use ref, out, and in parameters in C#?
description: Passing by reference safely: mutation, mandatory assignment, defensive copies, and modern ref-like alternatives.

data.text: **Question:** When do you use ref, out, and in parameters in C#?

All three pass arguments by reference instead of copying: **ref** passes a mutable reference in and out (the caller must initialize it first), **out** passes a reference that the method must assign before returning (output-only contract), and **in** passes a read-only reference (the method cannot modify it). Use them to avoid copying large structs, to return multiple values without allocating, or to express 'this method only reads'. In modern C#, `Span<T>`/`ref struct` and tuples have replaced most everyday ref/out usage — they shine in performance-critical code and interop.

**The three modifiers:**
- **ref**: bidirectional. Caller initializes before the call; callee reads and may write. `ref` locals and `ref` returns exist too (`ref int x = ref arr[0]` aliases without copying).
- **out**: output-only. Callee MUST assign before returning — the compiler enforces definite assignment. Caller doesn't initialize. Classic use: `TryParse`, `TryGetValue`, `DateTime.TryParse(s, out var dt)`.
- **in**: read-only reference. Callee sees the value as immutable; assigning to an `in` parameter of a struct creates a **defensive copy** — surprising cost on big structs. `in` is the safe way to pass a large struct without copying it *into* the method.

**Why they exist (value semantics of structs):**
- A struct parameter is copied by default — a 2 KB struct copied per call adds up in hot loops
- ref/in eliminate the copy; out lets a method fill a struct without a temp variable
- They also enable **multiple return values** pre-tuples: `static bool TryDivide(int a, int b, out double result)`

**Semantics and rules:**
- Arguments must match exactly at the call site: `M(ref x)`, `M(out y)`, `M(in z)` — you can't silently pass by value where ref is required
- `ref` and `out` don't participate in overloading (`M(ref int)` and `M(out int)` are the same signature)
- ref-safe contexts (C# 12): `ref struct` types, `ref` fields in ref structs — advanced territory for stack-only types like `Span<T>`
- `in` on a readonly field or with a literal creates a defensive copy — measure before using `in` on small structs (int, decimal)
- Tuples (`return (count, total)`) replaced most 'out for multiple values' cases; keep out for Try-parse-style APIs

**When NOT to use them:**
- Small types (int, Guid, small records) — copy is cheaper than the ceremony
- Async methods — **ref/out/in parameters are illegal in async methods** (the state machine can't hold them across awaits); use tuples or a result object instead
- Public API design: ref parameters make APIs awkward and prevent async variants

data.title: ref, out, and in side by side

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- The definite-assignment contract of out and the read-only contract of in
- Why structs motivate by-reference passing (copy cost)
- Awareness of the async restriction and the tuple replacement
- The defensive-copy gotcha with `in` on big structs

items: Using out parameters for multiple returns in new code — prefer tuples for readability
Assuming `in` prevents all copying — assignment to an `in` struct parameter copies
Trying to use ref/out in async methods — the compiler forbids it
Returning ref to a stack-only local — ref returns must reference still-valid storage
Overusing ref for small types where the copy cost is zero and the intent gets muddier
Confusing ref and out at the call site — out means 'the method owes me a value'
What is a defensive copy and when does `in` cause one?
What are ref structs and why can't they be boxed or used in async?
How do Span<T>/ReadOnlySpan<T> build on ref-like semantics?
Why can't ref parameters be used in iterator (yield) methods either?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: ref = in and out; out = callee must assign; in = read-only reference
By-reference passing avoids struct copies and expresses data flow
out/ Try-parse pattern is classic; tuples replaced most multi-return out usage
ref/out/in are banned in async and iterator methods
`in` can create defensive copies — measure on hot paths
data.takeaway: Use ref/in to avoid copying big values and out to return a computed value without an allocation — but reach for tuples and Span in everyday code first.
